drills.q: How large is a goroutine's starting stack, roughly, and does it grow?
drills.a: ~2KB, dynamically grown (and shrunk) by the runtime as needed, versus an OS thread's fixed 1-8MB reserved stack.

drills.q: True or false: sending on a closed channel returns the zero value silently.
drills.a: False -- sending on a closed channel panics. Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately with ok==false.

drills.q: Which Go release made GOMAXPROCS container-aware (cgroup-limit-based) by default?
A service's goroutine count and memory climb steadily under load with no crash or error log. What's the diagnosis process?
drills.a: Suspect a goroutine leak -- pull pprof's goroutine profile (/debug/pprof/goroutine) and look for a large number of goroutines sharing an identical blocked stack trace (same channel receive or lock), which is the diagnostic signature distinguishing a leak from a genuinely busy server doing varied work.

drills.q: Explain why `time.After(d)` called inside a `select` inside a `for` loop is a known anti-pattern.
drills.a: time.After allocates a new *time.Timer internally on every call, and that timer isn't eligible for GC until it actually fires. Calling it every loop iteration accumulates live-but-never-fired timers, producing steady memory and GC pressure in a hot loop. Fix: create one time.NewTimer outside the loop and Reset() it.

drills.q: Why is `defer cancel()` still required immediately after `context.WithTimeout()` even when you fully expect the deadline to fire on its own?
drills.a: Without calling cancel(), the context package's internal timer and cancellation-watching goroutine stay alive until the PARENT context itself ends, not until the current function returns -- a real, cumulative resource leak on the common path. cancel() is cheap and idempotent, so deferring it unconditionally is correct regardless of which path actually ends the context.

drills.q: State the Go memory model's happens-before guarantee for a mutex, and explain what it lets you safely assume.
drills.a: A sync.Mutex/RWMutex unlock happens-before a subsequent lock acquisition of the same mutex -- so any memory writes made while holding the lock are guaranteed visible to the next goroutine that successfully acquires it, without additional synchronization needed.

drills.q: Design a worker pool with N workers reading from a shared input channel and writing to a results channel, correctly handling context cancellation. What's the correct channel-closing sequence, and what breaks if it's wrong?
drills.a: The single producer goroutine feeding input closes the input channel (never a worker, to avoid a double-close panic); each worker selects on a channel receive alongside ctx.Done() to exit cleanly on cancellation; a separate goroutine calls wg.Wait() on all workers before closing the results channel. Closing results before all workers finish sending causes a 'send on closed channel' panic that manifests intermittently under real concurrent timing -- often passing in quick manual tests and failing under load.

drills.q: A `go test -race` suite passes cleanly in CI, but a data race ships to production anyway. Is this a contradiction? Explain.
drills.a: No contradiction -- the race detector only reports races that actually occur during the instrumented test run; it proves nothing about code paths the test suite never exercised or rare goroutine interleavings the run didn't hit. A clean -race run is necessary evidence, not sufficient proof of the absence of races across the whole codebase.

drills.q: A hot path shows unexpectedly high time in runtime.mallocgc in a pprof CPU profile. Walk through the diagnosis.
drills.a: Suspect escape analysis forcing a heap allocation the developer expected to be stack-local -- run `go build -gcflags="-m"` to see the compiler's actual per-variable escape decisions on that function. Common causes: a value returned by pointer, stored in a longer-lived structure, or passed through an interface method boundary the compiler can't statically resolve. Fix by restructuring to keep the value's lifetime provably local, if the allocation is genuinely avoidable.

drills.q: Write a generic constraint that accepts int, int32, int64, float32, float64, AND any named type built on one of those underlying types. What's the key syntax detail?
drills.a: type Number interface { ~int | ~int32 | ~int64 | ~float32 | ~float64 } -- the tilde (~) before each type is essential; without it, the constraint would only match the exact predeclared types and reject a named type like `type Meters int` even though its underlying type is int.
